title: Optimal Search Strategies under Finite Resource Constraints
abstract: Improving target search is a challenge faced by many natural and artificial agents, often requiring the use of energetic or material resources. These inputs may be supplied by an external controller or generated by the searcher itself, for example, through the deposition of cues along its trajectory. Although such resources are commonly modeled as costly but available without an explicit limit, in practice, they can often only be produced in finite amounts. Here, we go beyond the assumption of an unlimited supply of resources by investigating searches in which a finite resource budget must be allocated throughout the search process. To investigate this problem, we equip a one-dimensional diffusive searcher with three types of resources: an external force, a supply of partially reflecting flags, and auto-chemotactic cues. We derive exact optimal resource-allocation protocols for informed search processes in which the agent has continuous access to its past and current positions, which we find to always require resource allocation to be spatially concentrated. We then determine the corresponding protocols for blind searchers and show that resource usage must be more evenly distributed. Non-Markovian cues that generate environmental memory are found to substantially improve search performance when the agent has access to positional information, even under finite-resource constraints. In contrast, their benefits are considerably more limited for blind search, particularly when the cues provide no directional information.
summary: This work develops the theory of optimal search strategies when resources are scarce, moving beyond idealized unlimited resource assumptions. By modeling diffusion with external forces, deposited flags, and chemical cues, the authors derive protocols showing that positional knowledge allows for highly concentrated resource use. The findings highlight the critical difference in performance between informed and blind search strategies under resource limitations.
main_problem: The paper investigates optimal search strategies for an agent trying to locate a target when the resources required for the search (energy, materials, cues) are limited to a finite budget.
main_result: Optimal informed strategies concentrate resource allocation spatially, whereas blind searchers must distribute resources more evenly; non-Markovian cues significantly boost performance for informed search but less so for blind search.
method: The authors derive exact optimal resource-allocation protocols by minimizing the Mean First-Passage Time (MFPT) under finite resource constraints for various physical models.
model_or_system: The system models a one-dimensional diffusive searcher moving from $x=0$ to $x=L$, utilizing three resource types: an external force (Model I), deposited flags (Model II), and auto-chemotactic cues (Model III).
key_observables: Mean First-Passage Time ($ ar{T}$), optimal resource profiles ($	ext{c}^*(x)$ or $F(x)$), and the ratio $ ar{T}_{	ext{bl}} /  ar{T}_{	ext{inf}}$.
important_parameters: Finite resource budget ($W$ or $R_0$), diffusion constant ($D$), and the coupling strength ($ eta$).
main_assumptions: The analysis explicitly moves beyond the standard assumption of unlimited resource supply, considering fixed, finite budgets.
figures_summary: Figure 1 sketches the three resource models on a semi-infinite line. Figure 2 illustrates the optimal resource profiles for informed processes and the trajectory-averaged profiles for blind processes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes three distinct physical models (Force, Flags, Cues) to derive optimal resource allocation protocols for both informed (position-aware) and blind (stochastic) search processes, comparing the resulting MFPTs.
why_interesting: The concepts of optimal resource allocation and path-dependent memory effects in search processes are highly relevant to understanding energy minimization in complex physical systems, such as reaction-diffusion fronts or particle trapping in engineered potentials.

(c) Continuous cues can be deposited by the searcher and its further motion is governed by the cue profile gradient.
